description:
FringeLABS is a team based in Kerala, India, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our team brings together an interest in technology, scientific research, and software development, with a focus on building practical solutions to real-world challenges.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are developing Analog Finder, a platform designed to identify Earth locations that resemble the conditions of moon & mars.
summary: Analog Finder takes a landing region on the Moon or Mars and finds the places on Earth whose measured environment comes closest. A Python pipeline pulls NASA POWER climate data and LOLA and MOLA topography, builds a 0.1 degree grid over about 2.2 million land cells, and scores every cell against the target with a Gaussian similarity kernel on seven features: slope, relief, roughness, mean surface temperature, day to night swing, coldest surface temperature and annual precipitation. A Monte Carlo over perturbed weights reports how stable each rank is, so a site that only appears because of one weighting choice is visible as such. The results drive a 3D web terminal with Earth, Moon and Mars globes, similarity heatmaps for every target and preset, and a dossier per site holding the feature breakdown, an elevation profile and satellite links. Every value carries its source. The aim is to build physical intuition about which earthly places resemble a given landing region, and to show the working.
details:
What it does

Pick one of 12 landing regions, eight Artemis III candidate regions near the lunar south pole and four Mars sites (Jezero, Gale, Oxia Planum, Mawrth Vallis), then pick a weighting preset. The app returns the 50 best matching places on Earth, each with a score, the similarity for all seven features, the measured values behind that score, a rank-stability percentage from the Monte Carlo, an elevation transect and a hillshade chip. A 3D globe shows the target and the candidates together, a heatmap view shows the whole planet for that target and preset, and a split view puts the target terrain next to the Earth site. Satellite deep links open the same coordinates in Google Earth and NASA Worldview.

How it works

The Earth grid is built once. ETOPO 2022 bedrock elevation provides terrain and NASA POWER daily reanalysis provides climate, resampled to a 0.1 degree grid over land only. Terrain features are computed at a 28 km radius so that Earth and the target are compared at the same physical scale.

For each target, the pipeline reads a 28 km window of the global LOLA or MOLA elevation model and computes the same terrain features. A median despike removes single-pixel artefacts left by gaps between laser tracks; without it the de Gerlache window reports 27 km of relief instead of 11.5 km. Thermal values for the target come from published measurements, each with a citation recorded in config/targets.yaml, and the app displays that citation next to the number.

Scoring uses one Gaussian kernel per feature. A difference equal to the feature tolerance scores 0.61, twice the tolerance scores 0.14, and the weighted mean of the seven similarities is the site score. Weights come from four presets (polar, volcanic, dry basalt, cold desert) and are normalised inside the scorer.

Duplicate suppression removes candidates closer than 200 km and keeps a spread across continents, so the top ranks are not fifty cells on one ridge. The Monte Carlo perturbs every weight by up to 30 percent across 400 seeded draws and reports the share of runs in which a site stays in the top ten. The whole run is deterministic and reproducible.

The interface

React and TypeScript on Vite, with Three.js through globe.gl for the globes, D3 for charts, BluePrint JS for controls and Zustand for state. The build is entirely static: JSON, heatmap PNGs, hillshade chips and globe textures are bundled, and a SHA-256 manifest lists every file, so the app runs with the network switched off. It is deployed as a static site on Vercel and can be served from any CDN.

What we deliberately left out

Gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, the dust regime and Sun geometry are displayed but never scored. Adding them would reward an Earth site for having an atmosphere, which no Earth site can change. The score answers which environment is closest, and the app labels the non-scored values as context.

Solar elevation is computed against a flat horizon. At the lunar poles the Sun stays within about six degrees of the horizon, so real terrain shadows decide whether a site is lit, and every solar figure in the app carries that caveat.

Validation against eight known analog testbeds (Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Atacama, MDRS, HI-SEAS, Askja, Danakil, Lanzarote) put a testbed in the top 5 percent of Earth cells in 24 of 144 site, target and preset checks. Those testbeds were chosen in the literature partly for logistics, so a miss says the model did not rank a site highly, and it does not prove the site is a poor physical analog. The report is visible in the app.

One Artemis III region is missing. NASA lists nine, and the IAU Gazetteer gives a single centre point for the Mons Mouton massif, so the massif and the plateau cannot be anchored to distinct authoritative coordinates. We dropped that region rather than invent a coordinate.

Tools and languages

Python 3.13 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, netCDF4, Pillow, PyYAML, requests, SciPy-based scoring, scikit-learn and SpiceyPy for ephemerides. The app is React 18, TypeScript, Vite, globe.gl and Three.js, D3, Blueprint and Zustand, with Vitest for the frontend and pytest for the pipeline. Data comes from NASA, USGS, NOAA, Natural Earth and the IAU.

Why it matters

Analog sites are used to test instruments, suits and procedures before launch, and the reasoning behind a choice is usually buried in a report. This tool makes the comparison explicit: which features matched, by how much, with which source, and how sensitive the ranking is to the weights. It is useful for teaching, outreach and early mission-concept work, and it is honest about its own limitations.
